title: Web Development
summary: Go from "how does a web page even load?" to planning, building, securing and publishing a real full-stack site, with runnable HTML pages in every lesson.

lessons.title: How the web works
lessons.summary: Follow a web page from the moment you type an address to the moment it appears.

slides.title: The web in one sentence
slides.text:
The web is **computers asking other computers for files** and showing the result.
- Your browser is the **client**
- The computer that answers is the **server**
- They talk using **HTTP**
slides.narration: The web sounds magical, but the core idea is simple. A program on your computer, the browser, asks another computer, the server, for some files. The server sends them back, and the browser turns them into the page you see.

slides.title: From name to address
slides.text:
You type **example.com**.
1. **DNS** turns the name into an IP address
2. The browser opens a secure connection (**HTTPS**, TLS)
3. It sends an HTTP **request**
4. The server sends back a **response**
slides.narration: Computers find each other with numbers called IP addresses, so first the browser asks the Domain Name System to translate the name into a number. Then it opens an encrypted connection, sends a request, and waits for the response.

slides.title: A request and a response
slides.text: Every request has a **method** and a **path**. Every response has a **status code**, headers and a body.
slides.code:
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<!DOCTYPE html> ...
slides.narration: Here is what that conversation looks like as plain text. The browser says GET, which means please give me, followed by the path. The server answers with a status code. Two hundred means OK, four oh four means not found, and five hundred means the server itself had a problem.

slides.title: The browser builds the page
slides.text:
The HTML arrives first. Inside it the browser finds links to more files:
- **CSS** for the look
- **JavaScript** for behaviour
- **Images, fonts, video**
Each one is another request.
slides.narration: The first response is usually an HTML document. As the browser reads it, it discovers more files it needs, such as style sheets, scripts and images, and requests each of them. A typical page today makes dozens of requests.

slides.title: Front end and back end
slides.text:
- **Front end**: everything that runs in the browser (HTML, CSS, JS)
- **Back end**: code on the server (databases, logins, payments)
- **Full stack**: both
slides.narration: Web developers often split the work in two. The front end is what runs in the browser and what users touch. The back end runs on servers and handles data and business rules. People who do both are called full stack developers.

lessons.notes:
## The journey of a web page

When you visit a website, your **browser** (the client) talks to a **server** using **HTTP**, the HyperText Transfer Protocol. Today almost every site uses **HTTPS**, which is HTTP inside an encrypted TLS connection, so nobody in between can read or change the data. Modern browsers use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 under the hood, but the ideas below are the same.

## Step by step

1. **URL**: you type `https://example.com/about`. It has a scheme (`https`), a host (`example.com`) and a path (`/about`).
2. **DNS lookup**: the host name is turned into an IP address such as `93.184.215.14`.
3. **Connection**: the browser connects to that address and sets up encryption.
4. **Request**: it sends `GET /about`.
5. **Response**: the server replies with a status code and a body.
6. **Rendering**: the browser reads the HTML, fetches CSS, JavaScript and images, and paints the page.

## Status codes worth knowing

| Code | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| 200 | OK |
| 301 / 302 | Moved, go to another URL |
| 404 | Not found |
| 401 / 403 | Not logged in / not allowed |
| 500 | Server error |

## HTTP methods

- `GET` reads data
- `POST` creates something
- `PUT` / `PATCH` updates
- `DELETE` removes

## Try it

Open any site, press **F12** to open the developer tools and look at the **Network** tab. Reload the page and you will see every request, its status code and how long it took. This is the single most useful tool a web developer has.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns a domain name into an IP address
quiz.explain: DNS is the phone book of the internet: it maps names like example.com to IP addresses.

quiz.q: Which status code means "not found"?
quiz.explain: 404 means the server has nothing at that path.

quiz.q: Where does front-end code run?
quiz.explain: Front-end HTML, CSS and JavaScript run in the user's browser.

lessons.title: HTML, CSS and JavaScript together
lessons.summary: Learn the job of each of the three web languages and how they fit in one page.

slides.title: Three languages, three jobs
slides.text:
- **HTML**: structure and meaning (the skeleton)
- **CSS**: presentation (the clothes)
- **JavaScript**: behaviour (the muscles)
slides.narration: Every web page is built from three languages. HTML says what things are, like a heading, a paragraph or a button. CSS says how they look. JavaScript makes them do things when the user interacts.

slides.title: HTML: semantic structure
slides.text: Use tags that describe **meaning**: header, nav, main, article, button.
slides.code:
My Blog

Home

First post

Hello, web!
slides.narration: HTML uses tags in angle brackets. Good HTML is semantic, which means you pick the tag that describes the content. A real button element is better than a div that looks like a button, because screen readers and keyboards understand it.

slides.title: CSS: selectors and rules
slides.text: A **selector** picks elements, then **properties** style them. Custom properties (variables) keep colours consistent.
slides.narration: CSS is a list of rules. Each rule has a selector, which chooses the elements, and a block of properties and values. CSS variables, written with two dashes, let you define a colour once and reuse it everywhere.

slides.title: JavaScript: behaviour
slides.text: JavaScript finds elements and **reacts to events** like clicks.
slides.narration: JavaScript can find an element on the page, listen for an event such as a click, and change the page in response. Here every click increases a counter and updates the button text.

slides.title: Wiring them together
slides.text:
- CSS: a **link** tag in the head
- JS: a **script** tag with **defer**, or at the end of body
- Keep the three in separate files as projects grow
slides.narration: In a real project you keep the three languages in separate files. A link tag in the head loads the style sheet, and a script tag with the defer attribute loads JavaScript after the HTML has been read, so the elements already exist when your code runs.

lessons.notes:
## The three layers

| Layer | Language | Question it answers |
|-------|----------|---------------------|
| Content | HTML | *What is this?* |
| Presentation | CSS | *How does it look?* |
| Behaviour | JavaScript | *What does it do?* |

Keeping them apart is called **separation of concerns**. It makes pages easier to change, faster to load and friendlier to search engines and assistive technology.

## A typical file layout

```
my-site/
  index.html
  styles.css
  app.js
```

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>My site</title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
</head>
<body>...</body>
</html>
```

## Semantic HTML matters

Prefer `<button>` over a clickable `<div>`, `<nav>` for navigation, `<main>` for the main content and headings in order (`h1`, then `h2`...). Always give images an `alt` text. This is the foundation of **accessibility**: about one in six people live with some form of disability, and semantic HTML helps all of them for free.

## Modern CSS you can use today

All current browsers support CSS variables, Flexbox, Grid, `clamp()`, native nesting, `:has()` and container queries. You rarely need a preprocessor just to get these features any more.

## JavaScript basics

Use `const` and `let` (not `var`), arrow functions and template literals. Attach behaviour with `addEventListener` rather than `onclick="..."` attributes in HTML.

quiz.q: Which language is responsible for the look of a page?
quiz.explain: CSS controls colours, layout, fonts and spacing.

quiz.q: Why use a real button element instead of a styled div?
options: Keyboards and screen readers understand it
quiz.explain: Semantic elements come with built-in accessibility: focus, Enter/Space activation and a role.

quiz.q: What does the defer attribute on a script tag do?
options: Runs the script after the HTML is parsed
Loads it from a server only
quiz.explain: defer downloads in parallel and runs the script after the document has been parsed.

lessons.title: The DOM: changing pages with JavaScript
lessons.summary: Select, create and change elements, and respond to user events.

slides.title: What is the DOM?
slides.text: The **Document Object Model** is a live **tree of objects** the browser builds from your HTML. Change the tree and the page changes.
slides.narration: When the browser reads HTML it builds a tree of objects in memory called the DOM. Every element becomes a node with a parent and children. JavaScript cannot edit the HTML file, but it can edit this tree, and the screen updates instantly.

slides.title: Selecting elements
slides.text: Use **querySelector** with any CSS selector.
slides.narration: To work with an element you first need to find it. The querySelector method takes the same selectors you use in CSS and returns the first match. querySelectorAll returns all matches.

slides.title: Changing content and style
slides.text: Prefer **textContent** for text and **classList** for styles.
slides.narration: Once you have an element you can change its text, its attributes and its classes. Use text content for user-supplied text, because it never runs HTML. Toggle classes instead of setting many style properties, so the look stays in your CSS.

slides.title: Creating elements
slides.text: Build new nodes and **append** them to the tree.
slides.narration: You can also create brand new elements. Create one, fill it in, and append it to a parent. This is how to-do lists, chat messages and search results appear on a page.

slides.title: Events
slides.text: Listen with **addEventListener**. Use **event delegation** for many children.
slides.narration: Events are things that happen: clicks, key presses, form submits. You attach a listener function that runs when the event happens. For a form, call prevent default so the page does not reload. For long lists, put one listener on the parent and check which child was clicked. This is called event delegation.

lessons.notes: ## The DOM is a tree ``` document └─ html ├─ head │ └─ title └─ body ├─ h1 └─ ul ├─ li └─ li ``` Every box is a **node**. JavaScript reaches it through the global `document` object. ## Essential methods | Task | Code | |------|------| | Find one | `document.querySelector('.card')` | | Find all | `document.querySelectorAll('li')` | | Change text | `el.textContent = 'Hi'` | | Toggle a class | `el.classList.toggle('done')` | | Read an input | `input.value` | | Create | `document.createElement('li')` | | Insert | `parent.append(child)` | | Remove | `el.remove()` | ## textContent vs innerHTML `innerHTML` parses a string as HTML. If that string came from a user, they could inject a `

quiz.q: What is the DOM?
options: A tree of objects the browser builds from HTML
quiz.explain: The DOM is the live in-memory tree representing the page.

quiz.q: Why prefer textContent over innerHTML for user input?
options: It cannot run injected HTML or scripts
quiz.explain: textContent treats the value as plain text, preventing XSS.

quiz.q: What does e.preventDefault() do in a submit handler?
options: Stops the browser from reloading the page
quiz.explain: It cancels the default action, which for a form is navigating/reloading.

lessons.title: Fetch and APIs
lessons.summary: Load data from a server with fetch, async/await and JSON, and handle errors.

slides.title: What is an API?
slides.text: An **API** is a set of URLs a program can call to get or send data, usually as **JSON**.
slides.narration: An API, or application programming interface, is a door that one program opens for another. On the web, it is usually a list of URLs that return data instead of pages. The data is normally JSON, a simple text format that looks like JavaScript objects.

slides.title: JSON in one look
slides.text: JSON has objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null.
slides.narration: Here is some JSON. Curly braces hold an object with named keys, square brackets hold a list. In JavaScript, JSON dot parse turns text into objects, and JSON dot stringify does the opposite.

slides.title: fetch with async/await
slides.text: **fetch** returns a Promise. **await** waits for it without freezing the page.
slides.narration: The fetch function asks a URL for data and returns a promise, a value that will arrive later. Inside an async function you can await it, which reads like normal top to bottom code while the browser stays responsive.

slides.title: Handle errors
slides.text: Networks fail. Check **res.ok** and wrap calls in **try/catch**. Show a friendly message.
slides.narration: Important detail: fetch only rejects when the network itself fails. A four oh four or five hundred still counts as a response, so you must check res dot ok yourself. Wrap the call in try and catch, and always show the user something helpful instead of a blank page.

slides.title: Sending data and CORS
slides.text:
- POST with **method**, **headers** and a JSON **body**
- Browsers block cross-site reads unless the server allows it (**CORS**)
- Never put secret API keys in front-end code
slides.narration: To send data, pass an options object with the method, a content type header and a body. Two rules to remember. Browsers enforce CORS, so a server must explicitly allow other sites to read its responses. And anything in front end code is public, so secret keys belong on your server.

lessons.notes:
## REST APIs in short

Most web APIs follow a **REST** style: resources live at URLs and HTTP methods say what to do.

| Action | Method | URL |
|--------|--------|-----|
| List posts | GET | `/api/posts` |
| Read one | GET | `/api/posts/42` |
| Create | POST | `/api/posts` |
| Update | PATCH | `/api/posts/42` |
| Delete | DELETE | `/api/posts/42` |

Other styles exist, such as **GraphQL** (one endpoint, the client asks for exactly the fields it needs) and real-time **WebSockets**.

## Fetch pattern to memorise

```js
async function getJSON(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, options);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

// POST example
await getJSON('/api/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hello' })
});
```

## Three states of every request

Design your UI for **loading**, **success** and **error**. Users should never stare at an empty screen wondering what is happening.

## CORS

A page on `site-a.com` cannot read responses from `api.site-b.com` unless that server sends an `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header allowing it. This protects users. If you see a CORS error, the fix is on the **server**, not in your fetch call.

## Secrets

Anything shipped to the browser can be read by anyone. Keep API keys on a back end and have your front end call your own server.

## Offline note

The example below fetches a `data:` URL so it works without internet. Replace it with a real API address when you are online.

quiz.q: What does fetch return?
quiz.explain: fetch returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object.

quiz.q: A server replies with 404. What does fetch do?
options: Resolves normally; you must check res.ok
quiz.explain: fetch only rejects on network failure. HTTP errors are normal responses with ok set to false.

quiz.q: Where should a secret API key live?
quiz.explain: Everything in the browser is visible to users, so secrets must stay server-side.

lessons.title: Responsive design
lessons.summary: Make one page look great on phones, tablets and desktops with Flexbox, Grid and media queries.

slides.title: One site, every screen
slides.text:
More than half of web traffic is on phones.
- Design **mobile first**
- Use **fluid** sizes, not fixed pixels
- Add **breakpoints** where the layout breaks
slides.narration: People visit your site on phones, tablets, laptops and huge monitors. Responsive design means one page that adapts to all of them. The usual approach is mobile first: design for the small screen, then add rules as space grows.

slides.title: The viewport meta tag
slides.text: Without it, phones pretend to be a desktop and shrink your page.
slides.code: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
slides.narration: This single line in the head tells mobile browsers to use the real device width. Forget it and your carefully designed mobile layout will appear tiny and zoomed out.

slides.title: Flexbox and Grid
slides.text: **Flexbox** lays things out in one direction. **Grid** handles rows and columns together.
slides.narration: Flexbox is perfect for a row of buttons or a navigation bar. Grid shines for whole page layouts and card galleries. This grid line creates as many columns as fit, each at least two hundred pixels wide, with no media query at all.

slides.title: Media and container queries
slides.text: Media queries react to the **screen**. Container queries react to the **parent box**.
slides.narration: A media query applies rules only when the screen is at least a certain width. Container queries, supported in all modern browsers, let a component adapt to the space its parent gives it, which makes reusable components much easier.

slides.title: Fluid type and images
slides.text: Use **rem**, **%**, **clamp()** and **max-width: 100%** on images.
slides.code:
h1  { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem); }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
slides.narration: Finish with fluid sizes. The clamp function picks a font size between a minimum and a maximum that grows with the screen. Images get max width one hundred percent so they never overflow. Test by dragging the window narrower, and use the device mode in developer tools.

lessons.notes: ## Mobile first Write base CSS for small screens, then use `min-width` media queries to enhance for larger ones. Small-screen CSS is usually simpler, so this keeps your code lean. ```css .layout { display: grid; gap: 1rem; } /* phone: one column */ @media (min-width: 768px) { .layout { grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr; } /* tablet+: sidebar */ } ``` ## Units | Unit | Relative to | Use for | |------|-------------|---------| | `px` | nothing | borders, tiny details | | `rem` | root font size | font sizes, spacing | | `%` | parent | widths | | `vw` / `vh` | viewport | hero sections | | `dvh` | dynamic viewport height | full-height mobile layouts | Using `rem` for text respects the user's browser font-size setting, which is important for accessibility. ## Flexbox or Grid? - **Flexbox**: one dimension, content decides sizes (nav bars, button rows, centring). - **Grid**: two dimensions, layout decides sizes (pages, galleries, dashboards). ## Responsive images ```html ``` The browser picks the smallest file that looks sharp, saving data on phones. ## Testing Open developer tools and switch on **device mode** to preview many screen sizes. Then test on a real phone; touch targets should be at least about 44 by 44 pixels.

quiz.q: What does mobile first mean?
options: Writing base styles for small screens, then enhancing for larger ones
Building an app before a website
quiz.explain: Mobile first starts simple and adds min-width media queries.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for a two-dimensional card gallery?
quiz.explain: Grid manages rows and columns together.

quiz.q: What does a container query respond to?
options: The size of a parent container
quiz.explain: Container queries let a component react to the space its container provides.

lessons.title: Frameworks: React, Vue and Svelte
lessons.summary: Understand why frameworks exist, how components and state work, and how the big three compare.

slides.title: Why frameworks?
slides.text:
Large apps have lots of **state** (data that changes).
Updating the DOM by hand gets messy. Frameworks let you:
- describe the UI as a function of state
- split it into reusable **components**
slides.narration: With plain JavaScript you must remember to update every part of the page whenever data changes. In a big app that becomes a tangle. Frameworks flip the idea: you describe what the page should look like for the current data, and the framework updates the DOM for you.

slides.title: React
slides.text: Most widely used. Components are **functions** that return **JSX**. State via **hooks**.
slides.narration: React, from Meta, is the most popular choice. A component is a function that returns JSX, which looks like HTML inside JavaScript. The use state hook gives a component memory. React 19 and frameworks like Next dot js add server components and server side rendering.

slides.title: Vue
slides.text: Approachable, with **single-file components**: template, script and style together.
slides.code:
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const count = ref(0)
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="count++">Clicked {{ count }} times</button>
</template>
slides.narration: Vue is known for being friendly to beginners. A single file component keeps the template, the script and the styles in one file. Its reactive references update the page automatically when they change. Nuxt is its full stack framework.

slides.title: Svelte
slides.text: A **compiler**: turns components into small plain JS. Svelte 5 uses **runes** for state.
slides.code:
<script>
  let count = $state(0);
</script>

<button onclick={() => count++}>
  Clicked {count} times
</button>
slides.narration: Svelte takes a different route. It is a compiler, so most of the framework disappears at build time and you ship small, fast code. In Svelte five, state is declared with runes such as the dollar state rune. SvelteKit is its full stack framework.

slides.title: Choosing (and not choosing)
slides.text:
- Learn **plain HTML, CSS, JS first**
- Pick one framework and go deep
- Many sites need **no framework** at all
- Tooling: **Vite**, **TypeScript**, npm
slides.narration: All three are excellent and the concepts transfer: components, props, state and events. Learn the fundamentals first, then pick one, often React for job openings or Vue or Svelte for simplicity. And remember that a simple content site may need no framework at all.

lessons.notes:
## Core ideas shared by every framework

- **Component**: a reusable piece of UI with its own markup, logic and style.
- **Props**: inputs passed from a parent to a child component.
- **State**: data inside a component that can change; changing it re-renders the UI.
- **Declarative rendering**: you describe *what* the UI looks like for some state; the framework works out *how* to update the DOM.

## Comparison (2026)

| | React | Vue | Svelte |
|--|-------|-----|--------|
| Made by | Meta + community | Evan You + community | Rich Harris + community |
| Syntax | JSX in JS/TS | HTML templates, single-file components | HTML-like components, compiled |
| State | `useState`, hooks | `ref`, `reactive` | runes: `$state`, `$derived` |
| Full-stack framework | Next.js, React Router | Nuxt | SvelteKit |
| Strength | Huge ecosystem, most jobs | Gentle learning curve | Small, fast output |

Angular (Google) is also widely used in large companies, and lighter tools such as Astro (content sites that ship little JavaScript) and htmx (HTML-driven interactivity) are popular too.

## The modern toolchain

- **Node.js** runs JavaScript outside the browser and powers the tools.
- **npm / pnpm** install packages.
- **Vite** is the fast dev server and bundler most frameworks use.
- **TypeScript** adds types and is the default in most new projects.

```bash
npm create vite@latest my-app   # pick React, Vue or Svelte
cd my-app && npm install && npm run dev
```

## Advice

Frameworks change every few years, fundamentals do not. If you understand the DOM, events, fetch and CSS layout, you can learn any framework in a couple of weeks.

quiz.q: What is "state" in a UI framework?
options: Data that can change and causes re-rendering
quiz.explain: State is changing data; when it changes, the framework updates the UI.

quiz.q: Which framework works mainly as a compiler?
quiz.explain: Svelte compiles components into small plain JavaScript at build time.

quiz.q: Which is the full-stack framework built on React?
quiz.explain: Next.js is built on React; Nuxt is for Vue and SvelteKit for Svelte.

lessons.title: Back-end overview
lessons.summary: See what happens on the server: languages, routes, databases, authentication and APIs.

slides.title: What the back end does
slides.text:
- Stores data in a **database**
- Checks **who you are** (authentication)
- Enforces **rules** (you cannot buy what is out of stock)
- Talks to other services (payments, email)
slides.narration: The back end is the part of a website users never see. It keeps data safe in a database, checks who you are, enforces business rules and talks to other services like payment providers. The browser cannot be trusted with any of this, because users can change anything that runs on their machine.

slides.title: Popular back-end stacks
slides.text:
- **JavaScript/TypeScript**: Node.js, Bun, Deno with Express, Fastify, Hono
- **Python**: Django, FastAPI, Flask
- **Others**: Java Spring, C# ASP.NET, Go, PHP Laravel, Ruby on Rails
slides.narration: Almost any language can run a back end. JavaScript with Node is popular because you use one language everywhere. Python with Django or FastAPI is loved for its clarity. Big companies often use Java, C sharp or Go. The concepts are the same in all of them.

slides.title: Routes and handlers
slides.text: A **route** maps a method and path to a **handler** function.
slides.narration: A back end is mostly a list of routes. Each route says: when a request with this method and path arrives, run this function. The function reads the request, does the work and sends a response, often JSON.

slides.title: Data and authentication
slides.text:
- **SQL** databases: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite
- **NoSQL**: MongoDB, Redis
- Logins: hashed passwords, **sessions** or **tokens**, passkeys
slides.narration: Most back ends keep data in a database such as PostgreSQL. For logins, never store plain passwords: store a slow hash made with a tool like bcrypt or Argon2. After login, the server remembers the user with a session cookie or a token. Passkeys are a newer, phishing resistant way to sign in.

slides.title: Where back ends run
slides.text:
- Traditional **servers** or **containers** (Docker)
- **Serverless** functions
- **Edge** functions close to users
- Managed platforms handle scaling
slides.narration: Your back end can run on a rented server, inside containers, or as serverless functions that start only when a request arrives. Edge functions run in data centres close to the user for speed. Managed platforms handle scaling, so beginners can focus on code.

lessons.notes:
## Why a back end?

Anything in the browser can be read and modified by the user. So the server must:

- **Validate** every input again, even if the front end already checked it.
- **Authorise** every action: is this user allowed to delete this post?
- **Keep secrets**: API keys, database passwords.

## Request lifecycle on the server

1. Request arrives (`POST /api/orders`).
2. **Middleware** runs: parse JSON, check the session, log the request.
3. The **route handler** validates input and runs business logic.
4. It reads or writes the **database**.
5. It returns a **response** with a status code and JSON.

## A tiny Python API (FastAPI)

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
posts = [{"id": 1, "title": "Hello"}]

@app.get("/api/posts")
def list_posts():
    return posts
```

## Authentication vs authorisation

- **Authentication**: *who are you?* (password, passkey, sign in with Google)
- **Authorisation**: *what may you do?* (roles, ownership checks)

## Rendering choices

- **Client-side rendering (CSR)**: server sends JSON, the browser builds the page.
- **Server-side rendering (SSR)**: server sends ready HTML, faster first paint and better for SEO.
- **Static site generation (SSG)**: pages are built ahead of time and served as files.

Modern frameworks such as Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit and Astro mix all three per page.

## Environment variables

Configuration such as database URLs and keys is passed through environment variables (e.g. `DATABASE_URL`), never committed to Git.

quiz.q: Why must the server validate input even if the browser already did?
options: Users can bypass or change any front-end code
quiz.explain: Front-end checks improve UX, but only server checks provide security.

quiz.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
options: Authentication is who you are; authorisation is what you may do
Authorisation is who you are; authentication is what you may do
quiz.explain: Authentication proves identity; authorisation checks permissions.

quiz.q: How should passwords be stored?
options: Encrypted with a key in the code
As a slow salted hash (bcrypt, Argon2)
quiz.explain: Slow salted hashes mean a database leak does not reveal passwords.

lessons.title: Planning a full-stack project
lessons.summary: Turn an idea into a plan: features, data model, API, pages, stack and milestones.

slides.title: Start with the problem
slides.text:
Write one sentence: **who** is it for and **what** does it help them do?
Then list features as **must have**, **nice to have**, **later**.
slides.narration: Every good project starts with a clear problem, not a technology. Write one sentence about who the app is for and what it helps them do. Then sort features into must have, nice to have and later. Your first version should contain only the must haves.

slides.title: Model the data
slides.text: List the **entities**, their fields and how they relate.
slides.code:
User   (id, name, email, password_hash)
Book   (id, title, author, year)
Review (id, user_id -> User, book_id -> Book,
        rating 1-5, text, created_at)
slides.narration: Next, think about data. What things does your app store, and how are they connected? For a book club app you might have users, books and reviews. A user writes many reviews, and a book has many reviews.

slides.title: Design the API
slides.text: Each must-have feature becomes one or more **endpoints**.
slides.code:
GET    /api/books
GET    /api/books/:id        (with reviews)
POST   /api/books/:id/reviews   (logged in)
POST   /api/auth/login
POST   /api/auth/logout
slides.narration: Now turn features into API endpoints. Listing books, viewing one book with its reviews, and posting a review. Writing this list early lets front end and back end work in parallel.

slides.title: Sketch the pages
slides.text:
- Wireframe each screen on paper first
- Home, book page, login, profile
- Note **loading**, **empty** and **error** states
slides.narration: Before writing any CSS, sketch each screen on paper or a simple design tool. Boxes and labels are enough. Remember the states people forget: what the page shows while loading, when a list is empty, and when something fails.

slides.title: Pick a stack and milestones
slides.text:
Example: **SvelteKit or Next.js + PostgreSQL**, deployed on a managed host.
1. Static pages with fake data
2. Real database and API
3. Login
4. Polish, tests, launch
slides.narration: Choose tools you know or want to learn, and keep it boring and proven. Then plan small milestones that each end with something that works. Build the pages with fake data first, then connect a real database, then add login, then polish and launch.

lessons.notes:
## The planning checklist

1. **Problem statement**: "A book club app that helps friends share short reviews."
2. **Users**: who they are, what devices they use.
3. **Features**, sorted with MoSCoW: *Must, Should, Could, Won't (for now)*.
4. **Data model**: entities, fields, relationships.
5. **API**: endpoints, methods, who can call them.
6. **Pages and wireframes**, including loading, empty and error states.
7. **Stack**: front end, back end, database, hosting.
8. **Milestones**: small, demo-able steps.

## Minimum viable product (MVP)

An MVP is the smallest version that solves the core problem. Shipping it early teaches you more than months of planning.

## Choosing a stack in 2026

| Need | Sensible default |
|------|------------------|
| Mostly content | Astro or a static site generator |
| Interactive app | Next.js, Nuxt or SvelteKit |
| Python team | Django, or FastAPI + a front-end framework |
| Database | PostgreSQL (SQLite for small or local apps) |
| Auth | Your framework's auth library or a managed provider |

Pick **boring, well-documented** technology. You will learn faster when answers are easy to find.

## Project structure

```
book-club/
  README.md        <- what, why, how to run
  src/
    routes/        <- pages and API endpoints
    lib/           <- shared code, db access
  tests/
  .env.example     <- names of required env variables, no real secrets
```

## Use version control from day one

Create a Git repository before the first line of code, commit often with clear messages, and push to a remote such as GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg so you never lose work.

quiz.q: What should an MVP include?
options: Only the features needed to solve the core problem
Nothing until the back end is perfect
quiz.explain: A minimum viable product is the smallest useful version.

quiz.q: Why design the API list early?
options: Front-end and back-end work can proceed in parallel against a shared contract
quiz.explain: An agreed API is a contract both sides can build against.

quiz.q: Which states do people often forget to design?
quiz.explain: Real apps spend time loading, sometimes have no data and sometimes fail.

lessons.title: Web performance
lessons.summary: Measure and improve loading speed with Core Web Vitals, smaller files, caching and lazy loading.

slides.title: Why speed matters
slides.text:
Slow pages lose visitors and rank lower in search.
Google's **Core Web Vitals**:
- **LCP** loading (under 2.5 s)
- **INP** responsiveness (under 200 ms)
- **CLS** visual stability (under 0.1)
slides.narration: Every extra second of loading makes people leave. Google measures real user experience with three Core Web Vitals. Largest contentful paint measures how fast the main content appears. Interaction to next paint measures how quickly the page reacts to clicks. Cumulative layout shift measures how much things jump around.

slides.title: Measure first
slides.text: Use **Lighthouse** and the **Performance** panel in developer tools. Test on a slow phone profile.
slides.narration: Never guess, measure. Lighthouse, built into Chrome developer tools, gives a score and a list of fixes. The performance panel shows exactly what the browser was doing. Always test with network and CPU throttling, because your fast laptop is not your users phone.

slides.title: Ship less
slides.text:
- Compress images: **AVIF**, **WebP**, right size
- Minify and **bundle-split** JS
- Remove unused libraries
- Fonts: limit weights, use **font-display: swap**
slides.narration: The fastest byte is the one you never send. Images are usually the biggest files, so use modern formats and the right dimensions. Send only the JavaScript a page needs. Every library you add has a cost, so ask whether you really need it.

slides.title: Load smart
slides.text: Lazy-load below-the-fold images, reserve space, and defer scripts.
slides.narration: Tell the browser what matters. Images further down can load lazily. Give images a width and height so the layout does not jump when they arrive. Load scripts with defer so they never block the page from showing.

slides.title: Cache and CDN
slides.text: Use a **CDN** and long **cache** headers for files with a hash in their name.
slides.narration: A content delivery network copies your files to servers around the world so they travel a shorter distance. Build tools add a hash to file names, so you can tell browsers to cache them for a year. When the file changes, its name changes too.

lessons.notes:
## Core Web Vitals (2026)

| Metric | Measures | Good |
|--------|----------|------|
| **LCP** Largest Contentful Paint | When the main content is visible | ≤ 2.5 s |
| **INP** Interaction to Next Paint | Delay after clicks and key presses | ≤ 200 ms |
| **CLS** Cumulative Layout Shift | Unexpected movement | ≤ 0.1 |

INP replaced the older FID metric in 2024.

## Biggest wins, in order

1. **Images**: right size, AVIF/WebP, `loading="lazy"` below the fold, `width` and `height` always set.
2. **JavaScript**: ship less; split by route; avoid heavy libraries for small jobs; use `defer`.
3. **Caching**: hashed file names + `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable`.
4. **CDN**: serve static files from servers near users.
5. **Server**: fast responses, compression (Brotli or gzip), HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
6. **Fonts**: system fonts or few font files, `font-display: swap`, preload the main one.

## Keep the main thread free

Long JavaScript tasks block clicks and hurt INP. Break big work into smaller chunks, move heavy computing to a Web Worker, and avoid re-rendering huge lists.

## Measure with real users

Lab tools (Lighthouse) are great for debugging. Field data (real users) tells the truth. Many hosting platforms show Core Web Vitals from real visitors, and the `web-vitals` JavaScript library lets you collect them yourself.

## A performance budget

Agree on limits, for example "home page under 200 KB of JavaScript and LCP under 2 s on a mid-range phone", and check them in your CI pipeline so the site does not slowly get heavier.

quiz.q: Which Core Web Vital measures responsiveness to clicks?
quiz.explain: Interaction to Next Paint measures how quickly the page responds to input.

quiz.q: Why set width and height on images?
options: To make them load faster over the network
So the browser reserves space and the layout does not shift
It is required for alt text
quiz.explain: Reserved space prevents layout shift, improving CLS.

quiz.q: What does a CDN do?
options: Serves your files from servers close to users
quiz.explain: A content delivery network caches content at locations worldwide.

lessons.title: Web security basics
lessons.summary: Protect users from the most common attacks: XSS, CSRF, injection, weak passwords and leaked secrets.

slides.title: Think like an attacker
slides.text:
Rule one: **never trust input**.
Everything from the browser (forms, URLs, cookies, headers) can be faked.
The **OWASP Top 10** lists the most common risks.
slides.narration: Security starts with one rule: never trust input. Anything that comes from the browser can be changed by an attacker, including hidden fields and cookies. The OWASP Top Ten is a well known list of the most common web security risks, and it is worth reading.

slides.title: XSS: cross-site scripting
slides.text: An attacker gets **their script** to run on **your page**. Escape output, use textContent, add a **CSP**.
slides.narration: In cross site scripting, an attacker sneaks script into your page, for example inside a comment, and it runs in other users browsers. Prevent it by never inserting user text as HTML. Modern frameworks escape output by default. A content security policy header adds a second layer by blocking unexpected scripts.

slides.title: Injection
slides.text: Never build SQL or shell commands by gluing strings. Use **parameterised queries**.
slides.code:
# Dangerous
db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")
# Safe
db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))
slides.narration: Injection happens when user input is treated as code. The classic case is SQL injection. If you glue a user name directly into a query, a clever input can change the whole query. Parameterised queries send data separately from the code, which makes this impossible.

slides.title: Sessions, cookies and CSRF
slides.text: Session cookies: **HttpOnly**, **Secure**, **SameSite**. Protect forms against **CSRF**.
slides.code: Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
slides.narration: Session cookies should be marked HttpOnly, so scripts cannot read them, Secure, so they only travel over HTTPS, and SameSite, so other sites cannot send them along. Cross site request forgery tricks a logged in browser into submitting a request. SameSite cookies plus anti CSRF tokens stop it.

slides.title: The everyday checklist
slides.text:
- **HTTPS** everywhere
- Hash passwords (Argon2, bcrypt); offer **passkeys** / 2FA
- Secrets in env variables, never in Git
- Keep dependencies **updated**
- Check **permissions** on every request
slides.narration: Most breaches come from simple mistakes. Use HTTPS everywhere. Hash passwords and offer passkeys or two factor login. Keep secrets out of your code. Update dependencies, because old libraries have known holes. And on every request, check that this user is allowed to do this thing.

lessons.notes:
## The OWASP Top 10 in plain words

The Open Worldwide Application Security Project publishes a list of the most critical web risks. Common entries include:

- **Broken access control**: users can see or change data that is not theirs.
- **Cryptographic failures**: data sent or stored without proper encryption.
- **Injection** (SQL, command, XSS).
- **Insecure design** and **security misconfiguration**.
- **Vulnerable and outdated components**.
- **Identification and authentication failures**.

## Defences you can apply today

### Output encoding (XSS)
Use `textContent`, or your framework's default escaping. Be very careful with `innerHTML`, `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (React) or `v-html` (Vue). Add a **Content Security Policy**:

```
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'
```

### Parameterised queries (SQL injection)
```python
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?", (email,))
```

### Access control
On the server, check ownership on every request:
```js
if (post.authorId !== req.user.id) return res.status(403).end();
```

### Passwords and login
Hash with Argon2id or bcrypt, rate-limit login attempts, support multi-factor authentication and **passkeys**.

### Cookies
`HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` for session cookies.

### Secrets and dependencies
Use environment variables, add `.env` to `.gitignore`, and run `npm audit` or enable automated dependency updates (Dependabot, Renovate).

## Security headers worth setting

`Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy`, and `frame-ancestors` (in CSP) to prevent clickjacking.

quiz.q: What is the best defence against SQL injection?
quiz.explain: Parameters keep data separate from SQL code.

quiz.q: What does the HttpOnly cookie flag do?
options: Sends the cookie only over HTTP
Prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie
quiz.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie, limiting damage from XSS.

quiz.q: A user changes the URL from /orders/5 to /orders/6 and sees someone else's order. What is this?
quiz.explain: The server failed to check that the order belongs to the user.

lessons.title: Publishing your site
lessons.summary: Put your site on the internet: hosting options, domains, HTTPS, deployment pipelines and SEO basics.

slides.title: Getting online
slides.text:
You need:
1. A **host** to serve the files or run the server
2. A **domain name** (optional at first)
3. **HTTPS** (free and automatic on most hosts)
slides.narration: To publish a site you need somewhere to host it, an optional domain name, and HTTPS. The good news is that for static sites, hosting is often free, and most platforms set up HTTPS certificates for you automatically.

slides.title: Static vs dynamic hosting
slides.text:
- **Static** (HTML, CSS, JS files): GitHub Pages, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Vercel
- **Dynamic** (server code + database): Vercel, Netlify, Render, Fly.io, Railway, cloud providers, a VPS
slides.narration: Static sites are just files, so any static host can serve them cheaply and quickly. If you have server code and a database, you need a platform that runs code, such as a serverless platform, a container host, or your own virtual private server.

slides.title: Deploy from Git
slides.text: Connect a repository. Every **push** builds and deploys. Every **pull request** gets a preview URL.
slides.code:
git add .
git commit -m "Add contact page"
git push origin main
# host builds: npm run build
# and publishes the dist/ folder
slides.narration: The modern workflow is deploy from Git. You connect your repository to the host. When you push to the main branch, it builds and publishes automatically. Many hosts also create a preview link for every pull request so teammates can try changes before they go live.

slides.title: Domains and DNS
slides.text: Buy a domain from a registrar, then point it at your host with **DNS records**.
slides.code:
Type   Name   Value
A      @      203.0.113.10
CNAME  www    my-site.example-host.app
slides.narration: A custom domain makes your site look professional. You rent it yearly from a registrar. Then you add DNS records that point to your host, usually an A record or a CNAME. Changes can take minutes to a few hours to spread.

slides.title: Be findable and keep it healthy
slides.text:
- Unique **title** and **meta description** per page
- **sitemap.xml**, **robots.txt**
- Accessible, fast, mobile friendly
- Monitor uptime and errors
slides.narration: Once live, help people find you. Give every page a clear title and description, publish a sitemap, and make the site fast and accessible, because search engines reward that. Finally, set up uptime monitoring and error tracking so you hear about problems before your users do.

lessons.notes:
## Hosting options (2026)

| Site type | Good choices |
|-----------|--------------|
| Static HTML/CSS/JS | GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel |
| Framework app (Next, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro) | Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Render |
| Back end + database | Render, Fly.io, Railway, AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, a VPS |

Free tiers change often, so check current limits before choosing.

## A typical deploy pipeline

1. Code lives in Git (GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg...).
2. Push to `main`.
3. The host runs your **build** (for example `npm run build`).
4. Tests and checks run (CI).
5. The output is published to a CDN.
6. Pull requests get **preview deployments**.
7. If something breaks, **roll back** to the previous deploy with one click.

## Environment variables

Configure secrets (database URL, API keys) in the host's dashboard, not in your repository.

## Domain and HTTPS

- Buy a domain from a registrar.
- Add the DNS records your host gives you (`A`, `AAAA` or `CNAME`).
- HTTPS certificates are issued automatically (usually via Let's Encrypt).
- Redirect `http://` to `https://` and pick one canonical address (with or without `www`).

## SEO and sharing basics

```html
<title>Averroes Cafe | Mint tea and fresh bread in Cordoba</title>
<meta name="description" content="Family cafe with homemade cakes.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/share.png">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/">
```

Also: one `h1` per page, descriptive link text, `alt` on images, a `sitemap.xml` and a `robots.txt`.

## After launch

Watch uptime, error logs and Core Web Vitals. Back up your database. Keep dependencies updated. A site is never "done"; it is maintained.

quiz.q: What is a preview deployment?
options: A temporary live URL built from a pull request
quiz.explain: Hosts build each pull request to its own URL so changes can be tested.

quiz.q: Which DNS record type points a subdomain to another host name?
quiz.explain: A CNAME aliases one name to another; A points to an IPv4 address.

quiz.q: Where should production secrets be configured?
options: In the host's environment variable settings
quiz.explain: Environment variables keep secrets out of code and Git history.
